Periodic Table

EARLY ATTEMPTS AT CLASSIFICATION OF ELEMENTS

Döbereiner's Law of Triads (1817)

  • Döbereiner observed that when groups of three elements with similar properties (which he named "triads") were arranged by increasing atomic mass, the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the average of the atomic masses of the 1st and 3rd elements.

Newland's Law of Octaves (1865)

  • Newland discovered that when elements are arranged in increasing order of their atomic mass, the 1st and the 8th elements showed similar properties and characteristics.
  • Newland arranged the elements in horizontal rows, with each row having 7 elements and compared this to the eight octaves of music (do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do).
  • He published his concept in 1864 and recognition was given in 1865.
  • Last element: Thorium.
  • Total number of elements: 56.

Limitations of Newland's Model

  1. 1. The law was not true for elements beyond Calcium. After calcium, every eighth element did not share similar properties to the first one.
  2. 2. Those elements that were discovered after Newlands' octaves did not follow the law of octave.
  3. 3. To fit elements into his table, Newland sometimes placed two elements in the same position, even when they had different chemical and physical properties. E.g. Cobalt and Nickel were placed in the same slot without considering their differences from Iron, which was placed far away, despite similarities.
  4. 4. The periodic table did not include noble gases because they were not discovered then.

Lothar Meyer

  • Meyer published his first periodic table in 1862, which included 28 elements.
  • He published an updated version in 1864, which included 50 elements.
  • He was the first to identify periodic trends in the properties of elements.
  • He plotted the atomic volume of an element against its atomic weight to show this pattern.
  • Father of Periodic Table: Dmitri Mendeleev.

Mendeleev's Periodic Table (1869)

  • The periodic table was created in 1869 by Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist and inventor.
  • He arranged the 63 known elements at the time in order of their increasing relative atomic masses.
  • He divided the table into 8 groups and 7 periods.

Mendeleev's Periodic Law

  • Mendeleev's law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses, meaning that when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, elements with similar properties repeat themselves at regular intervals.

Limitations of Mendeleev's Periodic Table

  1. 1. The position of hydrogen is not fixed.
  2. 2. The increasing order of atomic weight is not maintained.
  3. 3. Some elements in the same group differ in their properties.
  4. 4. Lanthanides and Actinides were not included in the table.

MODERN PERIODIC TABLE

  • It was given by Henry Moseley in 1913.
  • Moseley discovered that elements are best characterized by their atomic number (the number of protons in the nucleus) and not by atomic weight.
  • The modern periodic table contains: 18 Groups and 7 Period.
  • Groups (vertical lines) → 18
  • Periods (horizontal lines) → 7
  • Elements → 118
  • Naturally occurring elements → 94
  • s: Valence e⁻ s subshell → Group 1 & 2.
  • p: Valence e⁻ p subshell → Group 13 to 18.
  • d: Valence e⁻ d subshell → Group 3 to 12 (Transition Metals).
  • f: Valence e⁻ f subshell → Inner Transition Metals.
  • s and p-block elements are collectively called as Representative Elements.
  • Metals: s, p, d, f.
  • Non-metals: Only in p-block.
  • Metalloids (7): Only in p-block (Germanium, Arsenic, Antimony, Tellurium, Boron, Polonium, and Silicon).
Metalloids are chemical elements that have both properties of metal and non-metals.

Group Names

  • Hydrogen → Group 1A
  • 1st Group → Alkali metal
  • 2nd Group → Alkaline Earth metals
  • Group 15 → Pnictogens
  • Group 16 → Chalcogens
  • Group 17 → Halogens
  • Group 18 → Noble gas/Inert gas

Some Special Elements

  • Seaborgium → Z = 106.
  • Mendelevium → Z = 101.
  • Rutherfordium → Z = 104.
  • There are a total of 94 naturally occurring elements.
  • 1st man-made element: Technetium (Z = 43).
  • Heaviest naturally occurring element: Uranium (Z = 92).

Lanthanides and Actinides

  • They are collectively called as Inner Transition Metals (f-block).
  • Lanthanides: 57-71 → Period 6
  • Actinides: 89-103 → Period 7 } Group 3

Diagonal Relationship

  • This relationship is prominent among the lighter members of the 2nd and 3rd periods.
  • A diagonal relationship in the periodic table is when two elements that are diagonally adjacent in the 2nd and 3rd periods have similar properties.

Some examples of diagonal relationships include:

  • → Boron and silicon (they are both semiconductors)
  • → Li and Mg.
  • → Be and Al.
  • → C and P.

TRENDS IN PERIODIC TABLE

Ionisation Energy

  • Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from a neutral atom in its gaseous state.
  • Across a period (left to right): It increases across a period because it becomes harder to remove an electron from an atom with a higher nuclear charge and smaller atomic radius.
  • Down the group (top to bottom): It decreases down a group as the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and more easily removed.

Electron Affinity

  • The energy released when an electron is added to a neutral atom to form a negative ion is called electron affinity.
  • Across a period (left to right): It generally increases (becomes more negative) because of increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic size, making it easier for the atom to attract an extra electron.
  • Down the group (top to bottom): It decreases (becomes less negative) down a group due to increasing atomic size and shielding effect.

Electronegativity

  • Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom of a given chemical element to attract shared electrons (or electron density) when forming a chemical bond.
  • Across a period (left to right): It generally increases as atoms become more effective at attracting electrons due to increasing nuclear charge.
  • Down the group (top to bottom): It generally decreases as the outermost electrons are further from the nucleus and less strongly attracted.
  • Elements with highest electron affinity: Chlorine.
  • Elements with highest electronegativity: Fluorine.

Electronic Configuration

  • The electronic configuration is distribution of electrons of an atom or molecule in atomic or molecular orbitals.
  • The K, L, M, and N shells represent the first four energy levels (or principal quantum numbers, n = 1, 2, 3, 4) where electrons are distributed, with K holding a maximum of 2, L holding 8, M holding 18, and N holding 32 electrons.

  • Rb = 2n²; K: 2; L: 8; M: 18; N: 32 (8, 1)

Octet Rule

  • The Octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to prefer to have 8 electrons in the valence or outermost shell. When atoms have fewer than 8 electrons, they tend to react to achieve a stable electronic configuration.
  • Octet Rule was given by Lewis and Kossel in 1916.

Isoelectronic Species

  • Isoelectronic species are atoms, ions, or molecules that possesses the same number of electrons, and therefore the same electronic structure, even if they differ in nuclear charge.
  • E.g. Oxygen, Fluorine, Magnesium.
₈O²⁻₉F⁻₁₂Mg²⁺
101010
Atomic Mass is represented as: amu or u

Calculation of Atomic Mass (A)

  • When protons (Z) is even, the number of neutrons (N) → 2Z.
  • When protons (Z) is odd, the number of neutrons (N) → 2Z + 1.

Exceptions: ₁H → 1, ₄Be → 9, ₇N → 14, ₁₈Ar → 40

Valency

  • Valency is the combining capacity of an atom, indicating how many electrons and atom can lose, gain, or share to form a stable compound.
  • ₁₁Na → 2, 8, 1 → 1e⁻ → Na⁺ → Losing an e⁻.
  • ₁₇Cl → 2, 8, 7 → 1e⁻ → Cl⁻ → Gaining an e⁻.

Variable Valency

  • It is the ability of certain elements, particularly transition metals, to exhibit more than one oxidation state or valency in different compounds. E.g. Fe → 2, 3; Ag; Cu (all transition metal show variable valency due to incomplete filling of f-orbitals).

Valence Electrons

  • Valance electrons are the electrons present in the outermost shell (valance shell) of an atom. These electrons determine the chemical properties and reactivity of the element.

Valency Based on Valence Electrons

  • If an element has 1, 2, 3 or 4 valence electrons → its valency is equal to the number of valence electrons. E.g. Elements in Group 1 (like hydrogen and sodium) have 1 valence electrons, so their valency is 1.
  • If an element has 5, 6, 7 or 8 valence electrons → its valency is calculated as: 8 − No. of valence electrons. E.g. Elements in Group 16 (like oxygen and sulphur) have 6 valence electrons, so their valency is 8 − 6 = 2.

Writing Chemical Formula of a Compound

  • E.g. Aluminium Chloride: AlCl₃; Carbon Tetrachloride: CCl₄
  • Al (3) Cl (1) — cross; C (4) Cl (1) — cross

Duet Rule

  • Duet Rule states that atoms like Hydrogen (H) and Helium (He) achieve stability when they have two electrons in their valence shell (K shell). To attain this stable configuration, atoms, either gain, lose, or share electrons by forming bonds with other atoms. E.g. In a water (H₂O) molecule, hydrogen shares electrons with oxygen to achieve a stable duet configuration.

CONCEPT OF ATOMICITY

Atomicity

  • Atomicity is the number of atoms present in a single molecule of an element or compound.

Diatomic Molecules

  • The substances that have two atoms in their molecules are called diatomic molecules.
  • There are only 7 elements that form stable homonuclear diatomic molecules and mostly exists as gases.
  • They are: Oxygen, Nitrogen, Hydrogen, Chlorine, and Fluorine, Bromine, Iodine. So diatomic is atomicity of non-metals too.

Monoatomic Molecules

  • The substances that are made up of single atom and lacks any covalent bond are called monoatomic molecules.
  • E.g. Helium, Neon, Argon, Krypton, Xenon, Radon.

Triatomic Molecules

  • The substances formed of molecules that are made up of three atoms are called triatomic molecules.
  • E.g. Water, Carbon dioxide, Hydrogen cyanide.
  • Ozone is triatomic (O₃).

Polyatomic Molecules

  • All the molecules that are made up of four or more atoms are known as polyatomic molecules. E.g. One molecule of sulphur is made up of 8 molecules, and one molecule of phosphorus is made up of 4 molecules. So both sulphur and phosphorus are polyatomic molecules.

Examples: S₈ ring structure; S₈ crown shape.
